title: Hayden Panettiere’s Estranged Mom Speaks Out After Actor’s Death: She ‘Lost Her Way’ and ‘I Wish She Had Stayed True to Herself’
description:
Hayden Panettiere’s estranged mother and former manager, Lesley Vogel, has spoken out about her daughter’s shocking death at the age of 36.

	In an
body:
Hayden Panettiere’s estranged mother and former manager, Lesley Vogel, has spoken out about her daughter’s shocking death at the age of 36.

	In an interview with NBC News, Vogel said, “I think Hayden was an amazingly talented person in so many departments and I think young people who grow up in the entertainment industry — it is a struggle and it’s a very challenging industry and it’s not unusual for them to sadly find the wrong path. I think it becomes very difficult to be true to yourself, and I think Hayden sadly lost her way, and I wish it were different. I wish she had stayed true to herself because she had many incredible attributes.”
	

	Panettiere detailed the turbulent relationship with her mother in her tell-all memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning” in May. Vogel, a former soap opera actress, was Panettiere’s manager when she started out in Hollywood at a young age. In her memoir, Panettiere called her mother a “perfectionist” and alleged that Vogel superglued a fallen tooth back into Panettiere’s mouth so she wouldn’t lose a job. She also claimed her mother pushed her to dress in more “girly” outfits, instead of her preferred tomboy style.


	When the memoir was released, Vogel told Page Six that she believed “the present drama is partially to sell books…As many parents of entertainment children [know], we are all too familiar with the painful observation of watching the self-destructive paths they sometimes choose. No parent hopes for this scenario; we want our children to be the best of themselves and live a peaceful, joyful life. Sadly, this is out of our control. You cannot save someone who does not want to be saved.”
	

	Regarding her mother, Panettiere told Us Weekly that “unfortunately, we don’t have a relationship right now” but “that doesn’t mean that I don’t leave the door open for the opportunity to present itself one day.” Vogel added in her NBC News interview, “I just feel that she’s with her brother and they’re at peace.” Panettiere’s younger brother Jansen died at 28 in 2023.

schema.headline: Hayden Panettiere’s Estranged Mom Speaks Out After Actor’s Death: She ‘Lost Her Way’ and ‘I Wish She Had Stayed True to Herself’

title: Motion Picture Academy Names Sean Baker and Samantha Quan as Chairs of Marquee Theater Committee
description: The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced Sean Baker and his partner, producer Samantha Quan, as the co-chairs of the new Marquee Th
body:
The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced Sean Baker and his partner, producer Samantha Quan, as the co-chairs of the new Marquee Theater Committee, which reviews submissions and recommends venues to be included on the Academy Marquee Theater List. 

	Additional chairs and vice chairs for the 2026-27 committees and affinity groups were also named, each serving a one-year term. The Academy’s committees and affinity groups are aimed to advance key initiatives and inform Academy policy while serving the interests of its memberships. 
	

	“As a member-led organization, we are deeply grateful to all our chairs and vice chairs for their leadership and engagement across the Academy’s work,” said Academy President Lynette Howell Taylor and Academy CEO Bill Kramer. “Their dedication helps advance our mission while ensuring that the Academy is well-positioned for the future.” 


	Baker won four Academy Awards in 2025 for his film “Anora.” Clockwork recently bought the distribution rights to Baker’s next project, “Ti Amo!,” which he previously told Variety was ”my love letter to the Italian sex comedies of the ’60s and ’70s.”

title: Frank Beard, Longtime ZZ Top Drummer, Dies at 77
description:
Frank Beard, ZZ Top‘s longtime drummer for the past 56 years, has died. He was 77.

	A representative for Beard confirmed that he died while in hosp
body:
Frank Beard, ZZ Top‘s longtime drummer for the past 56 years, has died. He was 77.

	A representative for Beard confirmed that he died while in hospice care at his ranch in Richmond, Texas, with his family by his side. Just last week, ZZ Top abruptly canceled their performance at the Hollywood Bowl due to Beard’s health issues. Last year, Beard temporarily stepped away from touring for similar reasons.


	In a statement shared with Variety, ZZ Top founder Billy Gibbons said, “Today, Elwood [Francis] and I lost a great friend and collaborator, and the world lost one of the most naturally innovative drummers and a great and true son of Texas. His signature backbeat was key to keeping ZZ on top. The band of which he was part for six decades is going to keep on keeping on as he had wished.”
	

	The band was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2004. The band’s co-founder, bassist Dusty Hill, died in 2021.

	While ZZ Top was best known for their synthesizer-powered 1980s hits, they were a thoroughly Texan, heavy rock-blues band at heart, spawned from the same psychedelic scene that birthed Roky Erickson and the 13th Floor Elevators but keeping things roots and rocking throughout their more than 50-year career, even as they incorporated synthesized rhythms into their sound in the 1980s.

	Though not a founding member of ZZ Top, Beard had played with the group since their debut “First Album” in 1971 through their most recent studio effort, 2012’s “La Futura,” as well as two recent live albums.  Although Gibbons and Hill were renowned for their flowing beards, Beard sported only a mustache; Gibbons famously said, “Frank’s beard is on his driver’s license.”
	

	Beard was born on June 11, 1949 in Frankston, Texas and was raised in Irving, Texas. Before joining ZZ Top, he performed in a variety of bands, often with Hill, including American Blues, the Warlocks, Hustlers and Cellar Dwellers. Beard replaced Dan Mitchell on the drums in ZZ Top in 1969 and helped recruit Hill from American Blues. The group’s classic lineup first performed in Beaumont, TX, on Feb. 10, 1970 and  remained the same for more than five decades: They celebrated their 50th anniversary at a San Antonio concert in February 2020.

	Launched on London Records in 1971, the trio secured its first major hit with the No. 8 LP “Tres Hombres” in 1973; the set included the raunchy single “La Grange,” a homage to the Chicken Ranch, the notorious bordello in the like-named Texas city. Another top 10 album, “Fandango!,” followed in 1975, powered by the FM-staple single “Tush.” Half of that album was recorded live in New Orleans, and captured the band’s powerful blues-rock groove.

	By the end of the ‘70s, ZZ Top’s potent brand of gutsy, no-frills blues ‘n’ boogie had made it one of America’s top concert attractions; its elaborate 1976 Worldwide Texas Tour featured actual livestock on stage. They moved from London Records to Warner Bros. in 1979 for “Degüello,” which shifted 1 million copies.

	While the popularity of “Degüello” hinted at bigger things to come, “El Loco” (1981) introduced both the sound and the look that would put the band over the top. The first hints of the sonic manipulation that would take center stage on “Eliminator” were heard on that set. Also, two years of tonsorial neglect between tours resulted in Gibbons’ and Hill’s long beards, which graced the album’s cover.

	But it moved to another level of popularity with 1983’s “Eliminator,” which found Gibbons and his band mates experimenting with new technologies – guitar loops, manipulated vocals and synthesized bass and drums — that refreshed their sound.

	The breakout success of three “Eliminator” singles – “Gimme All Your Lovin’,” “Sharp Dressed Man” and “Legs” – and their accompanying videos, which featured car aficionado Gibbons’ like-named 1934 Ford coupe, lofted the band to a new level of commercial success and popular ubiquity. In the wake of “Recycler,” the band was cast as themselves in Bob Zemeckis’ “Back to the Future III” (1990).
	

	“Eliminator” peaked at No. 9 and spent a remarkable 183 weeks on the American album charts, ultimately receiving diamond certification for sales of more than 10 million copies. The megahit album was succeeded by the quintuple-platinum “Afterburner” (1985) and the million-selling “Recycler” (1990).

	In 1994, ZZ Top exited Warner Bros. for a highly publicized $35 million pact with RCA Records. With that move, Gibbons took on co-production duties with the band’s longtime manager Bill Ham, who had helmed their studio work since the group’s debut single. The immediate result was the platinum album “Antenna.” Gibbons took the solo production reins on the group’s last two RCA releases, “XXX” (1999) and “Mescalero” (2003), and co-produced “La Futura” (2012) with Rick Rubin for his American Recordings imprint.

	The band continued a busy touring schedule into recent years, with the band’s longtime guitar tech, Elwood Francis, taking over for Hill — who had specifically requested before his death that Francis replace him — on bass. Gibbons, now 76, continues to perform regularly, although it was unclear at press time whether he will perform under the ZZ Top monicker.   

	Additional reporting by Jem Aswad.

schema.headline: Frank Beard, Longtime ZZ Top Drummer, Dies at 77

title: Round Hill Music Sues Suno, Anthropic for Copyright Infringement, Seeking Up to $1 Billion in Damages
description: The independent music publisher Round Hill Music sued Suno and Anthropic, accusing the two AI companies in a federal court in California of infringi
body:
The independent music publisher Round Hill Music sued Suno and Anthropic, accusing the two AI companies in a federal court in California of infringing its copyright by illegally scraping hundreds of its songs to train their models without permission.

	Round Hill, which owns the rights to songs such as Bonnie Tyler’s “Total Eclipse of the Heart, the Goo Goo Dolls’ “Iris” and more than 10,000 other compositions and recordings, claimed the two companies’ decision to lift the recordings violated the Copyright Act through its scraping. It listed 500 songs it alleged were part of the scraping, though promised that the complaint would be amended to reflect at least 10,000 songs pulled without permission. Such violations, it wrote, would demand damages in the “hundreds of millions of dollars and may ultimately approach or exceed $1 billion.”
	

	“We are not against artificial intelligence,” Round Hill CEO Josh Gruss said in a statement. “We are against the idea that you can build a business worth billions on top of other people’s creative work and pay the creators nothing. Licensing isn’t an obstacle to innovation – it is there to protect the legal owners of the raw material, their property.”


	Representatives for Suno and Anthropic did not respond to immediate requests for comment. 

	The lawsuit marks the latest filed against the two companies by a music publisher or label, reflecting the legally murky waters these companies operate in as they train and power their models. Suno has been sued by all three of the major labels – Warner Music Group, Universal Music Group and Sony Music – though it settled with WMG last year. Suno last week struck a licensing agreement with the music company BMG, which itself sued Anthropic earlier this year for allegedly using its recordings to train its models in what it called a scheme of “widespread and systematic infringement.”
	

	Round Hill Music is demanding a jury trial, signaling (at least for now) it has no intention to follow the other music companies in settling or striking a licensing agreement with the AI generators.

	“The question in these cases is not complicated,” said Richard S. Busch, the lawyer representing Round Hill Music who previously won the landmark music rights case against Robin Thicke’s “Blurred Lines” on behalf of the Marvin Gaye estate, in a sttaement.  Copyrighted works have been used to build multi-billion dollar businesses, and in the case of Anthropic a company now valued at more than a trillion dollars, while the songwriters and publishers who created the foundations of that value have received nothing. There is nothing fair about that use, and we look forward to making our arguments to the Court and in front of a jury.”

schema.headline: Round Hill Music Sues Suno, Anthropic for Copyright Infringement, Seeking Up to $1 Billion in Damages

title: Tyler, the Creator, Future, Leon Thomas to Perform at Camp Flog Gnaw 2026
description: Tyler, the Creator has released the lineup for his 12th annual Camp Flog Gnaw Festival, taking place at Los Angeles’ Dodger Stadium on November 14-1
body:
Tyler, the Creator has released the lineup for his 12th annual Camp Flog Gnaw Festival, taking place at Los Angeles’ Dodger Stadium on November 14-15.

	The rapper revealed the slate of performers via a website where fans had to unscramble letters for each act based on a particular hint. The internet was quick to figure out the entire lineup, which includes Future, Steve Lacy, Leon Thomas, Audrey Nuna, Lola Young, Wallows, Turnstile, Vince Staples, Don Toliver, Latin Mafia, Magdalena Bay, Earl Sweatshirt and Mike, Domo Genesis and many more. Tyler is, as always, featured on the lineup.
	

	Tickets for Camp Flog Gnaw 2026 are already sold out, but fans who weren’t able to secure passes can join a waitlist.


	The 12th annual event follows last year’s festival, which featured artists including A$AP Rocky, Clipse, Clairo, Childish Gambino, Doechii, Sombr, Thundercat, Malcolm Todd and many more. Tyler first staged Camp Flog Gnaw Carnival in September 2012 with a curtailed lineup that included Lil Wayne, Trash Talk and Odd Future, and expanded in the years that followed.

title: Laci Mosley’s ‘Scam Goddess’ Comedy Podcast Launches Video Episodes on YouTube, Joins Will Ferrell’s Big Money Players Network at iHeart
description: “Scam Goddess,” comedy podcast in which Laci Mosley and friends feast on crazy stories about frauds past and present, is now coming at you in video.
body:
“Scam Goddess,” comedy podcast in which Laci Mosley and friends feast on crazy stories about frauds past and present, is now coming at you in video.

	“Scam Goddess” has joined iHeartMedia and Will Ferrell’s Big Money Players comedy podcast network — and the show has expanded into video, with a new YouTube channel where fans can watch full-length episodes going forward.

	In each episode, Mosley — the self-proclaimed Queen of Scam — covers the hottest scams on the streets today while also breaking down the wildest robberies, grifts and assorted capers through history. Mosley is joined on the podcast to mull over the malfeasance by guests who have included Conan O’Brien, Jameela Jamil, Miranda Cosgrove, Lamorne Morris, Ayo Edebiri, Gayle King, JB Smoove, Nicole Byer and Matt Rogers.
	

	Mosley launched the “Scam Goddess” podcast in 2019. She penned a bestselling book of the same name that was published in 2024 and expanded the franchise with a Hulu original series that premiered last year. Mosley also staged a “Scam Goddess” sold-out national live tour with Live Nation. Her TV acting credits include “A Black Lady Sketch Show,” “Going Dutch” and “iCarly.”



	

	



	The first “Scam Goddess” video episode, “F.R.A.U.D. Is Dope the Jonathan Dupiton Con With Langston Kerman,” premieres today and features comedian and “My Momma Told Me” host Langston Kerman. He joins the show to break down AI ads, “beach ab” shots and the “shoddy merch” Jonathan Dupiton released for Dupiton’s podcast “Rich and Unemployed.”

	“Scam Goddess” is now available through Big Money Players, distributed by iHeartPodcasts via the iHeartRadio app and major podcast platforms. The first full-length video episode premieres Aug. 18 on YouTube. New episodes are released weekly on Tuesdays (and archive episodes are re-released each Friday).

title: Will David Ellison Say Goodbye to Hollywood? Some See Paramount’s Potential Exit From California as ‘Strategically Unwise’ — but Others Say It’s Just Smart Business
description: David Ellison, we have been told, loves Hollywood. He loves movies. In trying to rally industry support behind the Paramount-Warner Bros. megamerger
body:
David Ellison, we have been told, loves Hollywood. He loves movies. In trying to rally industry support behind the Paramount-Warner Bros. megamerger, he has claimed the combined studios will release an unprecedented 30-plus films a year. Waving the banner for the entertainment industry in his home state, Ellison also has been lobbying for bipartisan federal film tax incentive legislation, having met with Republicans in D.C. on the issue as recently as mid-July.
	

	And just a short time ago, Ellison was fully expecting to keep both Paramount and Warner Bros. in California. After outbidding Netflix in February to clinch the blockbuster deal, Ellison was queried by two prominent Democrats from the state — Sen. Adam Schiff and Rep. Laura Friedman — about his commitments to jobs in California.


	Ellison wrote in his reply that “my promise to you is to build a stronger Hollywood, by keeping both of these legacy studios operating separately, thereby preserving and potentially increasing jobs.” And this: “Paramount has deep roots in Southern California. My vision as a CEO is to stay true to our roots.”

	Well, that was then.

	Ellison has since become deeply frustrated with California politics. So much so that he recently told his senior-level team that Paramount will begin the process of pulling up stakes from the Golden State as soon as Oct. 1 unless the Warner Bros. Discovery merger is closed by the end of September — a deal that is currently on hold pending a 12-state antitrust lawsuit seeking to block it.

	The message that Ellison intends to take his business elsewhere seemed pointed directly at California attorney general Rob Bonta, who is leading the states’ lawsuit. Ellison wants the attorneys general to agree to hash out a settlement that would presumably let both sides save face — and close the deal before the case goes to trial in March 2027. At least publicly, Bonta has been unmoved. “Blackmail,” he called Ellison’s threat to move.
	

	On Monday, Paramount launched another bid to try to get the state AGs to the bargaining table, asking the judge overseeing the case to force the states and the WGA (which has also sued to block the Paramount-WB merger) to post a $1.88 billion bond. A rep for Bonta said Paramount was seeking a “do-over” on its agreement to delay the Warner Bros. Discovery merger until the antitrust trial: “They are lying in a bed of their own making, and once again, trying to blackmail us to get us to back down.”

	The lawsuits by the states and the WGA are the final obstacle to closing, after regulators in Mexico cleared the merger, leaving . Ellison said in a statement that “we have offered commitments and concessions and remain open to working constructively with the state AGs to find a path forward in the interest of our employees and the creative community in California and across the world.”

	But if Bonta and the attorneys general don’t engage, where will Ellison relocate? For now, the destination is unknown.

	States shortlisted for Paramount’s potential future home include Tennessee, Texas and Georgia. Note that Larry Ellison, who is backing his son’s merger bid to the tune of nearly $47 billion, moved Oracle’s HQ from California to Texas in 2020 and plans to move again to a massive new campus in Nashville. David Ellison owned a home in the Nashville area but sold it around the time the Skydance-Paramount merger closed in August 2025.

	Paramount employees fervently hope Ellison’s talk of a wholesale exit from Cali, including the studio operations, over a five-year time horizon is just saber rattling. One top exec, asked about the possible move, texted back a woozy-face emoji.

	“I hope this is saber rattling because I can’t think of anything that would less engender you to the population of this industry than to say you’re going to take Hollywood out of Hollywood,” Noah Wyle told Variety‘s Marc Malkin on Sunday. “But I’m an Angeleno, so I have a vested interest in that one.”

	At the same time, there’s a resigned feeling among some L.A.-based entertainment veterans that Paramount will indeed flee the state — and even sell the famed Paramount and Warner Bros. lots. As much as they dislike the idea, they don’t blame Ellison for what they characterize as an unsentimental but rational business decision. After all, if politicians in California are not going to step up with production incentives that are competitive with the likes of New York, New Jersey, the U.K. or Australia, why should production companies pay a premium to shoot in L.A.? That’s particularly true since filmmakers and actors are accustomed to traveling outside of SoCal these days.
	

	Ellison, at an Aug. 5 meeting with his senior team on the Paramount studio lot, claimed the company’s relocation could save some $500 million in taxes and other costs. However, Paramount’s income tax bill from California won’t change if it leaves, because state corporation taxes are apportioned based on where customers are located. “Unless you’re going to get all your customers to move, you’re not going to change how much gets sourced to California,” says Robert Johnson, who teaches state and local taxes at Cal State Northridge.

	According to sources familiar with the plan, Paramount expects to land big tax incentives from a new host state. It also anticipates paying workers less in a place with a lower cost of living than California, which in turn would reduce its payroll taxes.

	Any cost savings, though, would be offset by the significant expense of moving thousands of employees, not to mention building production sound stages elsewhere. Moreover, it’s likely many Paramount and WB workers would be unwilling to leave Southern California, if it came to that.

	For Paramount, decamping from L.A. would be “strategically unwise,” says JD Connor, a professor at USC School of Cinematic Arts. He points to “industry clustering” economic theory, which holds that industries like Silicon Valley and Hollywood are tied to their geographies because of the local talent pool.

	“You can continue to believe that the entertainment ecosystem can be disarticulated,” says Connor. “And yet it’s never taken hold. It turns out, it’s absolutely vital you go out to dinner with people.”

	Gene Maddaus contributed to this story.

schema.headline: Will David Ellison Say Goodbye to Hollywood? Some See Paramount’s Potential Exit From California as ‘Strategically Unwise’ — but Others Say It’s Just Smart Business

title: Emmys: A Breakdown of the Music Nominees From Lady Gaga’s ‘Dead Dance’ to Hans Zimmer’s Race for His First Win
description: Emmy’s music branch continues to welcome newcomers. Eighteen of this year’s 54 nominees, or one-third of the total in seven categories, are first-ti
body:
Emmy’s music branch continues to welcome newcomers. Eighteen of this year’s 54 nominees, or one-third of the total in seven categories, are first-timers to the competition. And only 12 are previous winners of TV’s highest honor.

	Composer Dave Porter, whose long professional relationship with creator-producer Vince Gilligan dates back to “Breaking Bad,” earned his first nominations for Apple TV’s “Pluribus”: music composition for a series, main title theme music, and (unusual for a composer) outstanding sound mixing for a series.
	

	Three other composers received two noms apiece: Jeff Beal, composition for a limited or anthology series plus main title theme for “All Her Fault”; Sean Callery, the same two categories for “The Beast in Me”; and Daniel Pemberton, composition for a series for “Slow Horses” and best song for “Spider-Noir.” Beal and Callery are previous Emmy winners.


	Film-scoring legend Hans Zimmer, who already has two Oscars and five Grammys, could finally win an Emmy (in his eighth time at bat) for co-composing the documentary score for “Prehistoric Planet: Ice Age.”

	This year’s statistics are a mixed bag. Only eight women were nominated (or 15%), down from nine last year; but 15 people of color (28%) received nominations, up from 24% last year. Also, 31 individual programs were chosen from 417 entries in the seven music categories, down from 480 entries last year.

	A first in the song category (officially “music and lyrics”) is “Mis Figuritas” from “Hacks,” the first-ever Spanish-language song to be nominated. And only five of the 31 programs nominated are from traditional broadcast networks—all in the music direction category.
	

	Final round voting takes place Aug. 17-26. Winners will be announced Sept. 5 and 6. Approximately 750 members of the TV Academy’s Music Peer Group are eligible to vote.

title: How the ‘Hacks’ Production Team Created a ’70s Sitcom Set and Overcame Las Vegas-Sized Challenges
description: In the “Hacks” universe, “Who’s Making Dinner?” is a fictional sitcom celebrating its 50th anniversary at PaleyFest with a screening and party. The
body:
In the “Hacks” universe, “Who’s Making Dinner?” is a fictional sitcom celebrating its 50th anniversary at PaleyFest with a screening and party. The story goes that the sitcom was created in the 1970s by Deborah (Jean Smart) alongside her late husband, Frank.

	However, Frank conned her out of a creator credit, leaving himself with sole writing credit. Between the PaleyFest celebration and the clips from “Who’s Making Dinner?,” “Hacks” production designer Rob Tokarz faced a challenge: “How do we make this?”
	

	Tokarz drew inspiration from classic sitcoms like “The Mary Tyler Moore Show” and “All in the Family,” that have endured and still resonate with audiences. “That’s where we started from. This show needed to feel as important,” he says.


	Tokarz drew from tones for the living room and décor from “All in the Family,” landing on a color palette of avocado shades, oranges and creams. “We wanted to live in that space with the wood paneling because it’s such a tip to that era. While we did pull out tones from ‘All in the Family,’ we wanted to uplift the actual architecture,” he explains. “And of course, when it comes to sitcoms, the couch is so incredibly important — it’s the focal point of just about everything we’ve ever seen.”

	Finding the right couch proved to be a mission.

	Jennifer Lukeheart, the show’s set decorator, searched far and wide. Ultimately, she found the seating in a surprising location: Facebook Marketplace. “It had the texture and tones that we were working with, and it had all the beats,” says Tokarz. The couch wasn’t all that paid homage to the past — the pass-through and doors used on “Hacks” were assets taken from the archives of TV history from the “Will and Grace” set, specifically from the episodes where the show honored “I Love Lucy.”
	



	

	



	As part of the PaleyFest sequence, Tokarz and his team took a few pieces from the set dressing and built that out.

	“We didn’t think the set walls would last, so we settled on photographing our set and blowing them up as photographic elevations,” he says. “It was the same scale as our set — just photographs.”



	

	



	Tokarz took pleasure in creating factoids that were featured throughout the exhibit, highlighting details about where a decorator may have found an item or the estate sale the clock was bought at in 1965 -“little details like that you never see on camera,” he says. They added gravitas to the history of the set.

	That set makes an appearance later on in the series finale, this time as Ava (Hannah Einbinder) walks around — but it looks very different. Tokarz updated it to make it feel contemporary, and approached it with realism.

	“We took the walls that we shot for ‘Who’s Making Dinner?’ We got rid of the wallpaper, repainted over the wood finishes, which is something that probably would have happened if that were a real space,” he says. “We have that shot where we’re echoing the beginning of Deborah’s journey. But now we’re in Deb’s legacy with Ava. Now Ava has her own legacy to build with her own show.”



	

	



	As it turned out, re-creating a set that paid homage to sitcoms of yesteryear was the least of Tokarz’s challenges.

	In episode 8, titled “The Cube,” Deborah stages a publicity stunt to announce her Madison Square Garden show. She’s still barred from performing due to the fallout from quitting her late-night show in Season 4, so she decides to have a magician suspend her in a Plexiglas cube above the Las Vegas Strip to announce the show.



	

	



	The sequence required the entire creative team to help solve the problem of how to pull it off, so it was shot in pieces and out of order.

	The episode was, at its core, a story about a box and a lot of creative problem-solving across all departments. Tokarz needed the cube to play both on stage in Los Angeles and on the Strip in Las Vegas, so the sequence was broken into three bits and, with the magic of VFX and editing, seamlessly woven together.

	The cube itself was made of steel and Plexiglas. “It sounds simple, but the actual construction needed to be engineer-stamped and approved because we were going to lift Deb up in it on stage,” Tokarz explains. “We had to get Plexiglas custom-made in Texas, and then make sure that all of the joints would work.”
	

	The cube also needed an eight-foot-wide door, which was engineered onto the structure with each pane weighing in at nearly 300 pounds.

	Considering the physics behind what happens when the door swings and the pressure it puts on the hinges, “it was all about finding the right hinge that would be able to maintain that,” he continues.

	But that was just the cube. The team then had to figure out how to re-create a blackout on the Las Vegas Strip, which occurs as Deborah is hoisted into the air in the cube. While it could not be done practically, Tokarz and his team built 130 feet of the Las Vegas Strip on a stage.



	

	



	“They’re not going to let you shut off enough lights, and there are way too many lights. Shooting on the actual Strip as a blackout wasn’t going to happen,” he says. So they found a solution. “We sent a team out. We matched every detail down to the joints in the sidewalk, the sprinkler heads and the balustrade on the wall. “We built olive trees from scratch so that they reflected the trees that they had at Caesars Palace.”

	The team spent a full day taking measurements, photographs, color samples and references. Making things even more challenging was that Formula 1 was setting up its Las Vegas circuit.

	“There were a lot of fences in the way, a lot of tape measures being thrown through chain-link fences to get measurements,” Tokarz recalls. “Then, we built it all on a soundstage.”

	First, the cube work on stage involved raising and lowering Deborah against a sea of solids to capture the visual effects elements, led by VFX supervisor Martin Hall.

	“We shot it in parts. We shot the visual effects elements of the cube on the soundstage, surrounded by solids. It was a really dark space with a lot of creative lighting elements,” Tokarz says. “The helicopter was really just a light on a rig that circled around to make sure she was lit properly. We had it going up and down so that we could match the camera angles.”

	The team also built a softbox enclosure, which was the size of an entire stage in order to properly light the scene.

	Once they had that lit and built, the ambulance and news trucks were brought onto the soundstage.

	But the true star of the scene was Hall. “He was our visual effects supervisor who did a fantastic job stitching it all together because all that had to make sense, and it was shot in three different elements,” says Tokarz. And it worked. “You just have to trust the process to come together.”

title: Nominated TV Producers Shed Light on Network Notes and Industry Changes at Variety’s Showrunners Breakfast; Ryan Murphy Emotionally Accepts Norman Lear Award
description: Hollywood’s top showrunners and creatives snuck out of their respective writers’ rooms for Variety’s annual Showrunner Breakfast on August 14. The i
body:
Hollywood’s top showrunners and creatives snuck out of their respective writers’ rooms for Variety’s annual Showrunner Breakfast on August 14. The intimate gathering was held at Oleander at The Sun Rose Hotel in West Hollywood, California, honoring top showrunners, including some listed in Variety‘s 2026 Showrunners Impact Report.

	As the room finished munching on their breakfast quiches and sipping cups of coffee, top showrunners and producers from Apple TV’s “Your Friends & Neighbors,” Netflix’s “The Diplomat,” Apple TV’s “Shrinking,” FX’s “Welcome to Wrexham” and Adult Swim’s “Rick and Morty” joined Variety‘s executive TV editor Michael Schneider for a panel discussing the timely topics on everyone’s minds — from network notes, the changing state of the writers’ room to AI.
	

	When it comes to navigating network notes, showrunners are often tasked with getting their version of the show across against what the network exec’s version might be. For “Your Friends & Neighbors” boss Jonathan Tropper, the most helpful notes ask about the writer’s intention.

	“You know, ‘I don’t know if that emotion is landing the way you think it is,’ or ‘I don’t understand, he seems to be acting like a dick here. Do you mean for him to be acting like a dick here?'” Tropper recalled. “Those are helpful because it’s somebody outside the brain trust reading it and reacting fresh. So I always divide notes into: Are they trying to write or direct the show? Or are they just trying to help me write the show?”

	Many of the panelists are hard at work on new seasons of their shows, including “Shrinking” executive producer Ashley Nicole Black, who has a lot to live up to after Season 3 nabbed 10 Emmy nominations.
	

	“It’s pretty daunting at first, but I find that once you make one decision, it sort of begets a bunch of other decisions,” Black said. “Now, in Season 4, Gabby’s moving into practicing a different kind of therapy, so we started working with a different therapist, Dr. Andrea Barthwell, who practices that kind of therapy. Once you start hearing her stories and her philosophies, the stories start to come out of that.”

	LISTEN to highlights from the Showrunners Breakfast on Variety‘s “Strictly Business” podcast

	“The Diplomat” showrunner Debora Cahn said it has taken her four seasons of working on the show to learn the most valuable lesson.

	 “I’m starting to get that the panic doesn’t go away because we’re still trying to do something we haven’t done. We’re still looking to do something slightly different and more,” Cahn said. “Panic is what it’s supposed to feel like.”

	“Rick and Morty” co-creator Dan Harmon heavily relies on his younger staff writers, especially to honor the canon of his show’s past seasons.

	“The kids, they go, ‘Well, I think Evil Morty should come back!’ And I say, ‘Says you, have fun writing that crap!'” Harmon quipped. “Thank God you’re here. Thank God we tend to promote our writers’ assistants so that they have everything on file.”

	Schneider ended the panel by bringing up the inevitable topic of AI. It’s of particular importance to these showrunners who work alongside the younger writers and assistants hoping to one day create their own show. But how will the next generation of showrunners fare?

	“It does start to feel like work is getting more and more temporary. A couple of years ago, it’d be like, ‘OK, I have to work on two or three shows a year.’ But there has to be two or three shows in order to make that work,” Black said.

	Tropper, meanwhile, said he “hesitates” to talk about AI because his mindset shifts based on the latest podcast or documentary he’s tuned into.

	“However fast we think it’s going to change things, it’s going to be faster,” Tropper said. “I cling to the hope that art will still have to be created by the vision of humans, and whether they’re using AI to realize that or not is going to fracture a lot of things.”

	The event closed out honoring Ryan Murphy, the prolific showrunner known for creating groundbreaking shows like “American Horror Story,” “Nip/Tuck” and “Glee,” with the Norman Lear Award. It was presented to him by another trailblazing showrunner in his own right, Greg Berlanti.
	

	While accepting the award, Murphy recalled how watching Lear’s landmark sitcom “All in the Family” helped him realize how television “can change hearts and minds.”

	“TV characters really become like friends, which we all know because they’re beamed at your house. And if you do it right, you can reach hearts,” Murphy said. “I got to tell Norman that story about the impact it had on me and how I realized so young that tackling important, if controversial, topics was necessary. And the amazing thing is when I told him that, he burst into tears like nobody had ever said a nice word to him in his life. But that was Norman.”

	Check out photos from Variety‘s Showrunner Breakfast below.

title: Hayden Panettiere Death: Brian Hickerson's Brother Found Her Unresponsive
description:
Hayden Panettiere
                          Boyfriend's Brother Found Her Unresponsive
body:
Hayden Panettiere
                          Boyfriend's Brother Found Her Unresponsive
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 18, 2026
                            12:30 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Brian Hickerson was asleep in another room when Hayden Panettiere went into cardiac arrest ... and sources tell TMZ it was Brian's brother who discovered her.
      
    
            Sources with direct knowledge tell TMZ ... Brian and Hayden were both inside an Airbnb in Greenville, South Carolina, Sunday afternoon -- when Zach Hickerson entered the residence and found Hayden in a chair in the living room.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            We're told at the time Zach arrived, Brian was sleeping in a separate bedroom.
      

            First responders were dispatched to the residence around 1:50 PM and attempted life-saving measures ... but Hayden could not be revived and was pronounced dead at 2:32 PM. Docs state Zach and Brian called 911.
      
    
            The police report said Brian was inside the Airbnb when Hayden died, though the circumstances surrounding his presence in the home were unclear at the time.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            Dispatch audio mentioned a possible overdose, and we know Narcan was found in the apartment.
      
    
            Hayden's cause and manner of death have not been determined. She was 36.

title: Hayden Panettiere Had Bag Full of Medication When She Died
description:
Hayden Panettiere
                          HAD BAG FULL OF MEDS WHEN SHE DIED
body:
Hayden Panettiere
                          HAD BAG FULL OF MEDS WHEN SHE DIED
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 18, 2026
                            10:04 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 18, 2026
                                12:34 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Hayden Panettiere had a bag full of medication when she died suddenly on Sunday ... and her boyfriend showed the meds to cops.
      
    
            According to the police report ... Hayden's boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, and his brother, Zach, were in the Greenville, SC, apartment when she died ... and Brian showed police the "bag of medication" Hayden was taking at the time of her death.
      
    
            The specific meds were not identified in the police report obtained by TMZ ... though it sounds like nine different drugs were redacted.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            TMZ broke the story ... Narcan was found in the apartment where she died. Narcan is administered nasally to reverse the effects of an opioid overdose, and we're told the device used to dispense it was found on a mattress.
      

            We're also told epinephrine was used on the scene, and that would line up with the initial 911 call for a woman in cardiac arrest. Epinephrine, aka adrenaline, is commonly used to resuscitate patients in cardiac arrest.
      
    
            Zach was reportedly "very emotional" while emergency medical services professionals were trying to save Hayden.
      
    
            As for Brian ... he reportedly didn't become visibly emotional until she was declared dead at the scene.

description:

                          We Wanted BF Brian Gone A Long Time Ago!!!
body:
Hayden Panettiere’s Mom
                          We Wanted BF Brian Gone A Long Time Ago!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 18, 2026
                            11:11 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 18, 2026
                                1:12 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Hayden Panettiere's estranged mom just broke her silence over her daughter's shocking death ... and she used the opportunity to dump on Hayden's boyfriend, Brian Hickerson.
      
    
            Lesley Vogel told NBC News ... "This person in her life that we have been trying to get rid of for quite some time was with her at her death, and that was Brian Hickerson."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            It's worth noting ... Brian loathed Lesley as much as she hated him ... telling TMZ back in May, "Hayden's mother is by far one of the worst people I've ever met in my life ... I just can't with her. She's terrible."
      
    
            As TMZ reported ... Brian and his brother Zach were at the scene when Hayden died on Sunday in a South Carolina apartment.
      

            Lesley says ... "I think Hayden was an amazingly talented person in so many departments and I think young people who grow up in the entertainment industry -- it is a struggle and it's a very challenging industry and it's not unusual for them to sadly find the wrong path." She doesn't out-and-out blame Brian for her death ... but she sure insinuates he was a bad influence.
      
    
            Brian and Hayden started dating in 2018, and they were on and off for years ... though we found out they had been keeping their rekindled romance under wraps during the release of her memoir because people in her camp felt he was bad for business.
      
    
            As TMZ reported ... Zach was reportedly "very emotional" while emergency medical services professionals were "working on Hayden."
      
    
            As for Brian ... the police report, as cited by NBC, says he didn't become visibly emotional until she was declared dead at the scene ... and he showed cops a bag of medication Hayden was taking at the time of her death.
